highlights.title: The locked test
highlights.question: Do the lead models hold up on a year they were never tuned on, run exactly once?
highlights.finding: Nine candidates ran a single time on the held-back year from 2025-11 to 2026-11, at live size, with fees, entry delays from 0 to 20 minutes and a 40% loss limit. A record written beforehand refuses a second run. Only trend_10_50_lock passed every rule.

highlights.title: Tuning hard to one year
highlights.question: How much can a trend model make if it's tuned as hard as possible to the past year, and what happens outside that year?
highlights.finding: A deliberate overfitting experiment. trend_hyper_593 made +149% on the year it was fitted to and lost 38% over the two and a half years before it, with a 76% worst drop. It trades on paper to see how a fitted model holds up live.

highlights.title: Cash out after a big day
highlights.question: Does closing everything and withdrawing the gain after a big day beat holding?
highlights.finding: No version beat holding in both periods. On the overfitted model it worked as a circuit breaker: banking 8% days and rejoining at the next close turned $1 into $1.70 over the whole span with a 25% worst drop, against $1.55 and a 76% drop for holding.

highlights.title: Bank 3% from the entry
highlights.question: Is a fixed rule of banking 3% from the entry, then rejoining at the next close, an edge?
highlights.finding: It lost to holding in both periods. A fixed 3% cuts short the big trend runs this model earns its money from, and measured from the entry it almost never fires in a losing stretch, so it protected less than the daily version. Judgement on when to bank has beaten the fixed rule on paper.

highlights.title: Positioning as a signal
highlights.question: Does the crowd's long/short positioning on Binance predict where price goes next?
highlights.finding: Fading the crowd when it was stretched made money in both periods tested, but failed two of the five rules set beforehand. It trades on paper as crowd_fade to build a live record. A small machine-learning blend of the readings and equal-risk sizing both failed.

highlights.title: Buying liquidation flushes
highlights.question: After a cascade of forced long liquidations, does price bounce enough to trade?
highlights.finding: The study found a bounce of about 1.35% a trade. A second check, entering about 65 seconds after the flush at a price that was really available, cut the expectation to about 0.70%. It trades on paper as liq_flush_buy.

highlights.title: Ten ways to lock in gains
highlights.question: Can trend_10_50_lock give back less of its open profit without hurting its return?
highlights.finding: Ten exits were tested one after another: tighter trails after a hot streak, account-wide profit locks, momentum and level exits, and finally stepping aside before squeezes. None beat the plain model by the rules set beforehand.

highlights.title: Size with the trend's strength
highlights.question: Does stepping a trade's size up as its trend strengthens beat a fixed size?
highlights.finding: It did no better than trend_10_50_ldss simply run at a bigger size. Its adds-only version trades on paper as trend_10_50_ldss_adds.

highlights.title: Candles as a language (Kronos)
highlights.question: Can an open foundation model that reads price candles like text call the past year's moves?
highlights.finding: Run locally on a consumer GPU, Kronos failed on direction, on the size of the move, and as a filter for the existing models.
